analysis.one_liner: Bars voter purges and challenges based on returned mail or unreliable list matches.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have stopped voters from being removed or challenged based on returned mail and unverified list matches, never received a Senate vote and died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped state and local election officials from removing a voter from the rolls or letting someone formally challenge a voter's eligibility when the only evidence is a piece of mail sent to the voter that came back undelivered, or a list that matched voters against people who are ineligible without solid proof the two entries are the same person. It would also have required anyone filing a challenge to state specific grounds under oath, with fines up to $50,000 for knowingly abusive challenges. The bill was referred to the Senate Rules Committee, which held a hearing in February 2008, but the committee never acted on it and it never got a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Registered voters, especially people who move often (renters, students, service members), low-income voters, and minority voters, who are disproportionately hit by mail-based purges and mass challenges. Election workers also benefit from clearer rules about what evidence counts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters at risk of wrongful purges

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits election officials from blocking a voter's registration or voting, or permitting a formal challenge, when the sole basis is a returned piece of nonforwardable mail, a document the voter did not send back, or a list generated by matching voters against ineligible people without a signature, photo, or unique ID number verifying the match.

Requires any private challenge to a voter's eligibility to state specific written grounds and be made under oath or attestation subject to penalty of perjury, and bars challenges based solely on caging documents or unverified match lists.
Imposes a fine of up to $50,000 for each knowing violation by someone who challenges a voter in violation of the act with intent to disqualify the voter.

analysis.who_pays: Parties and campaign operatives lose a cheap tactic for mass challenges; election officials must document legitimate grounds before acting on returned mail; a small number of people who file knowingly false challenges face fines.

drawbacks.text: Returned mail is sometimes a genuine sign a voter has moved, so states lose a low-cost way to identify and update outdated registrations, and election officials may need to spend more verifying eligibility before acting.

The bill gives a federal commission power to designate other types of evidence as insufficient on its own, which opponents of federal election rules generally view as an intrusion on state control of election administration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are narrow: they do not stop states from maintaining accurate rolls or from challenging voters for good reason, they just bar decisions based solely on returned mail or unverified data matches, methods that regularly misidentify legitimate voters. The cost is some extra verification work for election officials and the loss of a tactic that favored one side's campaign strategy. On balance the safeguards to individual voters outweigh the administrative burden.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Rules Committee, which held a hearing but never voted to send it to the floor, and it expired when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the Caging Prohibition Act of 2007 on November 5, 2007, with 14 Democratic cosponsors including then-Senators Obama, Clinton, Kerry, and Leahy.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration, which held hearings on February 27, 2008.
No further action was recorded; the committee never reported the bill and the Senate never voted on it before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Campaign operatives and party committees that use mass mailings and list matches to generate voter challenges keep the tactic. Voters targeted by those tactics gained nothing, and election officials got no added clarity.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote was ever taken; all 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but the bill died in committee before any recorded position could emerge.

industries.note: Mail-based 'caging' and unverified list matches are inexpensive ways to generate mass challenges that burden targeted voters on or before Election Day. The bill would have barred using that evidence as the sole basis for a challenge and fined knowing violations up to $50,000 each.
The bill constrains officials from acting on returned mail alone but codifies clear federal rules; it also leaves the National Voter Registration Act's protections fully intact.
